## Abstract

Background:

Surgical care centralization in the U.S. delays access and increases carbon emissions. Global targets

suggest patients live within 2-hours of a surgical facility. This study quantifies the environmental impact

of travel for cataract surgery in rural Michigan and models the potential emissions reductions from

decentralizing surgical and follow-up services.

Methods:

A retrospective, cross-sectional study analyzed electronic medical records from a rural Michigan

ophthalmology practice (March–November 2023). We calculated travel distances using population-

weighted centroids and estimated emissions using U.S. Department of Energy vehicle data. A k-means

clustering model optimized additional facility placement, and a gradient analysis identified optimal

numbers for decentralization points, for emissions reductions.

Results:

The 920 patients traveled a median of 55.45 km (IQR: 43.33–88.20 km) for surgery and 55.07 km (IQR:

43.54–87.82 km) for follow-up visits, generating Total Surgical Access Emissions (TSAE) of 57,168

kgCO� (median of 59.20 kgCO�; IQR: 32.31–81.87) under the centralized model. The k-means

decentralization model and gradient analysis identified 7 hospitals and 9 clinics, respectively, as the

optimal expansion points, reducing emissions by 34.07% (19,475 kgCO� saved) and 39.52% (22,590

kgCO� saved). The Surgical Access Carbon Impact (SACI) model demonstrated that achieving two-hour

access to clinic services reduced excess emissions by 54.7%. Sensitivity analyses using fuel-efficient

vehicles (Toyota Prius and Tesla Model 3) or reducing follow-up visit frequency reduced emissions by

54.03% (30,888 kgCO�) and 25.83% (14,768 kgCO�), respectively.

Conclusion:

Decentralizing surgical services in rural U.S. settings could cut travel-related emissions by up to 40%,

significantly reducing healthcare-related carbon footprints while improving timely access to care. The

SACI metric provides a novel framework for integrating environmental sustainability into U.S. health

policy and service planning.

## Introduction

Timely access to surgical care is essential for averting avoidable disability and death for both emergency

and elective surgical conditions [1]. However, access remains limited globally, including in rural regions

of high-income countries such as the United States. The concept of "surgical deserts," introduced by the

American College of Surgeons in 2009, highlights areas with inadequate surgical coverage that require

patients to travel long distances to receive care [2]. These travel demands create significant barriers in

terms of timely access and impose financial costs on patients and health systems [3]. In 2015, the Lancet

Commission on Global Surgery (LCoGS) set a benchmark stating that the entire population should live

within two hours of a facility capable of providing surgical care [1]. This access indicator has since

informed national surgical plans globally [4], yet it does not account for the environmental impact of long

travel distances.

Centralized care models-including centers of excellence-consolidate resources and expertise, but

frequently overlook the access challenges imposed on rural populations [5,6,7]. These models impose

travel burdens, leading to prolonged journey times, delays in care, and increased out-of-pocket expenses,

all of which exacerbate health inequities and contribute to worse outcomes for rural patients [8,3]. Travel

for care also carries environmental implications: long-distance travel is a key driver of greenhouse gas

(GHG) emissions [9]. While alternatives such as virtual follow-up are suitable for some conditions,

surgical procedures and their postoperative care generally require in-person attendance, compounding the

environmental cost of centralized delivery.

The environmental stakes are considerable. The U.S. healthcare sector accounts for approximately 10% of

national GHG emissions [10]. Patient healthcare-related travel alone generates an estimated 35.7

megatons of CO�-equivalent annually in the United States, representing 6.4% of total healthcare-sector

emissions [12]. Rural patients, who face longer distances, generate higher per-trip emissions than urban

counterparts [12]. Yet the carbon cost of surgical care delivery architecture-the geographic distribution

and organizational structure of services-has received little empirical attention.

This study quantifies the effect of decentralizing initial and follow-up surgical care on GHG emissions in

rural America, using cataract surgery as a representative model. We hypothesize that decentralization of

surgical services reduces patient travel-related carbon emissions.

This retrospective, cross-sectional study was conducted at a single ophthalmology practice located in a

rural area of Michigan, USA. The practice serves a catchment population of approximately 40,000

residents, with no other ophthalmic practices present in the surrounding four counties. The study includes

all patients who traveled to the practice and underwent elective cataract surgery (intraocular lens surgery -

IOL) at a hospital located in the same hospital complex, from March to November 2023. An IRB waiver

was obtained as this was not human subjects (IRB Protocol: 24-1130). We followed STROBE reporting

guidelines for observational studies.

Data Handling and Analysis

Data were collected from the electronic medical records (EMR) of the practice for the following

variables: procedure type, date of procedure, number of postoperative visits, and patient residence zip

codes. In this study, all procedures took place at the same facility and all postoperative visits occurred at

the same clinic. Calculated variables included distance traveled (km) and drive time (minutes). Distance

traveled was estimated as the round-trip from the population-weighted centroid of the zipcode where the

patient resides to the clinic or hospital, based on geographic data from Open Street Maps (OSM). The

OSRM function in R used Dijkstra’s algorithm, optimized with contraction hierarchies, as a way-finding

algorithm considering road classification and speed (motorways: 100 km/h, trunk roads: 90 km/h,

residential: 50 km/h for defined paths). ArcGIS Online was used for geographic visualization. All

calculations were performed using R Studio (version 2024.04.2+764).

Carbon Emission Calculations

Carbon emissions (in kgCO�) were estimated using data on vehicle types, fuel efficiency, and emission

factors. We obtained vehicle data in Michigan from publicly available sources to assume of the most

commonly registered car in the state - the Ford F-150 Series SUV (Michigan RMV). In addition, we

looked at the impact of driving the most fuel-efficient vehicles in Michigan, namely the Toyota Prius and

Tesla Model 3 respectively. All fuel economy data and corresponding greenhouse gas emission (GHG)

factors (in kilograms of CO� per mile) were obtained for model year 2022 from the US Department of

Energy.

Decentralized Care Model

A modified k-means clustering approach was used to optimize the placement of hypothetical additional

hospital and/or clinic locations. This method added n additional locations to the catchment area. The

initial n additional starting points were randomly selected amongst the 47 population-weighted zipcode

centroids, with small random offsets to their coordinates. Each population-weighted centroid was

assigned to the closest location and the total distance calculated. Each n point’s location was recalculated

according to a linear weighted average of the longitude and latitude positions. New coordinates’ were

weighted by patient count per zipcode in the assigned cluster. The total distance was recalculated

iteratively until convergence, which was defined as a < 1% change in total distance traveled. Recalculated

points outside the polygon of contiguous zipcodes were snapped to the nearest point within the polygon.

The end-point was set where an asymptote was observed in the decentralization model’s trajectory,

suggesting that further decentralization yielded minimal additional impact. For each decentralized model,

a Wilcoxon-rank-sum was used to compare the reduction of carbon emissions to the centralized model.

The inflection point for optimal reduction in total carbon emissions, based on n additional locations, was

defined as the value of n where the first derivative was positive or zero, or by a change in the sign of the

second derivative if the first condition was not met.

To assess the combined effect of decentralizing both surgical and postoperative care, we analyzed total

carbon emissions across permutations of n additional hospital and clinic locations. A gradient analysis

was performed to calculate the rate of change in total carbon emissions using the Carbon Emissions

Surgical Access Carbon Impact (SACI)

We proposed the Surgical Access Carbon Impact (SACI) metric to link the impact of achieving timely

access according to global safety targets, with changes in carbon emission. We set sequential timeliness

thresholds at 15, 30, 40, 60, 90 and 120 minutes and calculated the excess carbon emissions for patients

living outside the acceptable drivetime perimeter. We tested for significant differences in excess

emissions at the different drivetime thresholds using a Kruskall-Wallis test.

This study evaluates the carbon impact of decentralizing surgical care, specifically for cataract surgeries.

The results demonstrate that centralized care models impose environmental costs due to increased travel,

with the total emissions for all procedures and follow-ups under the current model reaching 57,167.62

The predominant approach to reducing healthcare's carbon footprint has focused on hospital energy

efficiency, pharmaceutical supply chains, and high-impact clinical inputs such as volatile anesthetic

agents [13,14]. Comparatively little attention has been paid to care delivery architecture—the geographic

distribution and organizational structure of services—as an environmental determinant. The OECD has

explicitly identified transforming healthcare delivery as a key decarbonization pathway, yet empirical

frameworks for doing so at the service-planning level remain scarce [15]. By demonstrating that the

spatial configuration of surgical facilities is a quantifiable driver of travel-related emissions, this study

provides an actionable, evidence-based lens through which planners can evaluate the environmental

consequences of care organization decisions.

Centralized healthcare delivery models have been widely adopted in their perceived efficiency in

consolidating expertise, resources, and advanced technologies. These models aim to improve patient

outcomes through specialized care and streamlined service delivery. However, the broader implications of

centralization to access to care, particularly for rural populations, are often overlooked. Centralized care

disproportionately impacts patients who live far from these centers, imposing significant travel burdens,

delays in access, and financial costs [16]. Although the facility and area described in this study was not

formally designated a ‘centre of excellence’, it was the sole provider of ophthalmologic surgery within the

catchment area, effectively functioning as a centralized facility and producing similar burdens on patients.

Cataract surgeries were selected for this study as a representative model due to their defined care cascade,

discrete and predictable care pathway, and reliance on in-person postoperative evaluations. These

characteristics make ophthalmologic procedures well-suited for exploring the interplay between care

delivery models and environmental impacts. The two clinics for postoperative follow-up form part of the

centralized service. Our findings demonstrate that decentralizing follow-up care through additional clinic

locations could reduce emissions by up to 39.52%, while decentralizing surgical care at the hospital level

could reduce emissions by up to 29.09%.

A central objection to surgical decentralization is that distributing procedures across more facilities risks

diluting volume per site, with adverse effects on quality. This concern is well-founded for high-acuity

complex procedures such as pancreatectomy, oesophagectomy, and complex cancer surgery, where robust

surgery, and by extension a wide range of high-volume, lower-acuity elective procedures, an appropriate

This study adds to the prevailing narrative around making healthcare more ‘green’ which focuses largely

on consumption of hospital facilities or the broader climate narrative around improving vehicle fuel

efficiency as a means of decreasing emissions. Without accounting for the carbon impact of patient travel,

centralization risks undermining broader sustainability goals, particularly in the context of global efforts

to reduce healthcare-related emissions [11]. Rural populations simultaneously bear the heaviest burden of

inadequate surgical access and generate the highest per-trip healthcare travel emissions [12,19]. Climate

change disproportionately affects rural communities through extreme weather events, agricultural

disruption, and infrastructure vulnerability, compounding pre-existing socioeconomic disadvantage [20].

Healthcare systems that impose long-distance travel on rural patients are simultaneously extracting access

equity from the patients themselves while extracting environmental capacity from communities least

equipped to absorb the cost. Geospatial adjustments in facility distribution, when paired with existing

efforts to change transportation types, offer a synergistic strategy for reducing emissions, particularly for

follow-up care [8,3]. However, we found that decentralization of care, particularly follow-up care, can

have a more substantial effect on overall vehicle emission reduction. This suggests that systemic

reorganization of healthcare delivery, including geospatial restructuring, could have broader

environmental and patient-centred benefits.

Population health access indicators play a pivotal role in bridging healthcare and climate policy.

Indicators like the LCoGS two-hour access benchmark are traditionally assessed through a population

health lens, evaluating how distance and travel time affect patient outcomes and timely intervention.

However, this study demonstrates that these access indicators also have environmental implications.

When populations are unable to access care within the two-hour threshold, longer travel distances

increase the carbon footprint of healthcare delivery. We proposed the SACI indicator as a practical way to

integrate access to care and climate impact for surgical care. While this study is grounded in a single rural

Michigan practice, the SACI framework and k-means facility optimization approach are procedure-

agnostic and geographically transferable. The analytical pipeline could be applied to any elective surgical

procedure with a defined care cascade including colonoscopy, hernia repair, or orthopaedic procedures,

## Limitations

This study is not without limitations. First, the absence of granular vehicle data required assumptions

about the most commonly used vehicles in the state. However, we include sensitivity analyses to provide

lower-bound estimates on the carbon savings from optimal healthcare center placement, assuming

everybody drove the most fuel-efficient vehicles available in Michigan at the time of this study. Secondly,

our use of population-weighted centroids to approximate travel distances may not fully reflect individual

travel patterns. Although the k-means clustering approach approximates optimal facility placement, it

does not guarantee a global minimum for emissions. Finally the study focuses on the climate benefits of

decentralization without considering the broader impact on specialized infrastructure and expertise only

available in centralized facilities; these domains are adequately addressed in other studies of

centralization. Additionally, we did not conduct a life cycle assessment (LCA) of the environmental

impact of building additional facilities, which could partially offset the emissions savings. Future research

should balance environmental considerations with known benefits of centralization, including clinical

safety, efficiency, and resource optimization. The findings here, however, lay the groundwork for a

comprehensive CBA approach by contributing a climate criterion to decision-making frameworks.

Policy implications

1. Optimize the number of facilities: Our analysis identified a local minimum configuration of

additional clinics and hospitals to achieve significant emission reductions and improved access to

care, with potential flexibility depending on population density and demand. This model should be

considered when planning for the expansion of the service delivery platform. While this model did

not account for the potential of increasing facilities to induce demand and increase patient visits),

future implementation of the model would require evaluation and patient behavior changes.

2. Incorporate climate metrics into access monitoring: Population health access indicators, like the

LCoGS two-hour threshold, should explicitly account for the environmental impact of unmet clinical

## Conclusion

Decentralizing surgical care delivery presents a significant and underrecognized opportunity to reduce the

carbon footprint of healthcare, particularly in rural areas. This study demonstrates that the spatial

organization of surgical services is a quantifiable, modifiable driver of travel-related emissions, reducible

by up to 40% through evidence-based facility planning. The SACI metric provides a novel framework for

integrating environmental sustainability into surgical care planning, and the analytical pipeline is

transferable to other procedures, settings, and national contexts. Meeting global surgical access

benchmarks and achieving healthcare sustainability goals are not competing imperatives.

## Abstract

Surgical care is essential to achieving universal health coverage (UHC) and addressing 30% of the global disease burden, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), maternal health and injuries. However, low and middle-income countries (LMICs) face significant challenges providing equitable access to surgical services, with 5 billion people lacking access and US$20 trillion in associated global economic losses, emphasising the need for sustainable domestic financing strategies.

A multifaceted approach combined quantitative analysis of domestic health spending trends (2000–2021) using the WHO Global Health Expenditure Database with illustrative case studies examining fiscal mechanisms. The quantitative analysis assessed government health expenditure (GHE), current health expenditure (CHE) and resource allocation. Illustrative case studies examined fiscal mechanisms, including taxes, subsidies, levies and public health insurance, drawn from published literature and policy reports in selected LMICs. A surgical expenditure surrogate (SES), defined as the proportion of health expenditure allocated to NCDs, reproductive, maternal, neonatal, child and adolescent health and trauma and injuries, was used as a proxy to estimate spending on surgical care.

In 2021, global CHE totalled US$9.84 trillion, with GHE contributing a global median of 53.66%. LMICs allocated only 34.88% of CHE to domestic resources, relying heavily on external funding and out-of-pocket payments. Using the SES as a proxy for surgical spending, spending on communicable diseases (CDs) outpaced SES in LMICs (median SES: 40.17% vs CD: 49.38% of CHE). Mechanisms like taxes, subsidies and public health insurance show potential to expand fiscal space but face challenges such as inequities, sustainability concerns and limited allocation to surgical care.

Strengthening domestic financing through targeted fiscal policies and improved resource allocation can enhance access to surgical care and health system independence in LMICs. National surgical plans and better reporting metrics are critical to integrating surgical care into UHC strategies.

## WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC

- Access to safe and timely surgical care is limited in most low and middle-income countries (LMICs), with persistent reliance on out-of-pocket payments and external funding. Governments play a central role in financing health systems, but domestic resource allocation for surgical care has historically been inequitable and understudied.

## WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS

- Using a multifaceted approach combining global health expenditure data and illustrative case studies, this study estimates surgical spending through a surgical expenditure surrogate and identifies fiscal mechanisms (such as taxes, subsidies, levies and insurance schemes) that could expand domestic fiscal resources for surgical care.

## HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY

- Findings highlight opportunities to strengthen government-led financing for surgical care, inform policies for more equitable and sustainable allocation of domestic resources and support the integration of surgical care into universal health coverage strategies.

## Introduction

Surgical care is an essential component of universal health coverage (UHC), yet most health systems in low and middle-income countries (LMICs) are unable to provide safe, timely and affordable surgical care to their populations.1 Five billion people lack access to surgical and anaesthesia care, leading to an estimated US$20 trillion (2010 US$, purchasing power parity) in global economic losses.2 Surgical care is central to the diagnosis and definitive management of 30% of the global disease burden including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), maternal, neonatal and child health conditions, and trauma and injury,3 all key targets of Sustainable Development Goal 3. In response, countries are developing national surgical plans (NSPs) to strengthen surgical systems. However, implementation is often slow and inconsistent, with lack of financing identified as a core barrier.4 5

Governments play a central and catalytic role in financing and coordinating health services, particularly in LMICs where they act as both provider and payer for much of the population.5 Expanding domestic fiscal space is, therefore, essential to facilitate effective and efficient health spending for safe surgical care.6–8 The WHO Global Health Expenditure Database (GHED) provides insight into the domestic fiscal space through measures of gross domestic product (GDP) per capita and the domestic government proportion of health expenditure, proxies for national capacity and commitment to finance healthcare.7 In many LMICs, national health budgets are stretched thin, with public health prioritisation focused on infectious diseases.7 9 Within Africa, only Cabo Verde and South Africa have met the Abuja Declaration (2001) target of allocating 15% of GDP to health.10 The domestic financing gap is compounded by limited prioritisation of surgical system strengthening and the lack of clear financing strategies.

Effective implementation of surgical policies and improvements in health system efficiency depend on a comprehensive understanding of how domestic resources are mobilised, pooled, allocated and spent—including government allocations, prepayment mechanisms and insurance schemes—to prioritise surgical care within health budgets and integrate surgery as a core component of UHC.11–14 This paper examines how domestic resources are mobilised, analyses allocation across disease priorities and surgical entry points and explores specific domestic financing mechanisms through selected case studies.

The study evaluated domestic health spending trends from 2000 to 2021, using freely available open-source data from the WHO GHED and additional country-specific reports. Illustrative case studies were used to contextualise quantitative findings by highlighting various domestic financing mechanisms for surgical care.

We developed a surgical expenditure surrogate (SES) to estimate the allocation of health expenditure towards surgical services in settings where direct surgical expenditure data are unavailable. SES is defined as the proportion of healthcare expenditure dedicated to three disease burden categories that commonly require surgical care: NCDs, reproductive, maternal, neonatal, child and adolescent health (RMNCAH) and trauma and injuries. These categories were selected because surgical intervention is frequently required across the continuum of care, such as operative management of malignancies and cardiovascular disease (NCDs), caesarean delivery and gynaecologic surgery (RMNCAH), and trauma and injury care. Communicable diseases were excluded given their predominantly medical management, consistent with recent expert-consensus classifications of operative conditions.15 While SES assumes a substantial proportion of expenditure within these categories involves surgical services, it overestimates true surgical spending, as the chosen categories also include non-operative care. Therefore, SES represents an upper-bound proxy for surgical expenditure, rather than a direct measure.

While we initially sought allocations for emergency, critical and operative care (ECO), current GHED data coding methods do not align with ECO classifications, necessitating a focus on operative (surgical) care. Patients were not involved in the design of this study.

### Data handling

The primary data source for this analysis was the WHO GHED, which provides health expenditure data for 194 countries from 2000 to 2021. Variables such as current healthcare expenditure (CHE), CHE as percentage of GDP, general government expenditure (GGE), domestic general government health expenditure (GGHED), voluntary prepayments (VPP) and out-of-pocket (OOP) payments were used (see online supplemental table A1 for a list of acronyms and online supplemental table A2 for the data dictionary). CHE represents total health spending from all sources within a country, including domestic and external financing. Domestic health expenditure comprises domestic government spending (GGHED) and domestic private spending (VPP and OOP), while GGE refers to total government spending across all sectors, including healthcare. Data were further disaggregated by country income categories as defined by the World Bank.16 For this study, LMICs were grouped together to preserve data completeness and statistical stability and to reflect the study’s focus on shared constraints in domestic health financing and surgical fiscal space, which are distinct from those in HICs. The year 2022 was excluded from this analysis due to the incomplete dataset available in GHED at the time of this study. Disease burden categories provided in GHED align with Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation guidelines. Corresponding variables from the WHO GHED database were used to identify spending on specific health areas (online supplemental table A1).

### Data analysis

The quantitative analysis focused on disaggregating healthcare expenditure data by source and allocation. Descriptive statistics (medians and IQR) were calculated to summarise health spending trends. All analyses were conducted using R Studio V.2024.04.2.

### Illustrative case studies

Direct comparisons of domestic financing mechanisms across countries using annual health budgets over 21 years were not feasible. To address this limitation, illustrative case studies in non-high-income countries with documented experience in expanding surgical fiscal space were selected to contextualise quantitative findings. Cases were chosen based on the availability of financing data, evidence of successful implementation of domestic financing mechanisms and to highlight variation in policy approaches and fiscal mechanisms across regions. Case studies were further organised by financing mechanism (taxes, subsidies, levies, insurance and OOP payments) to align with financing categories examined in the quantitative analysis and were identified from the existing literature (including grey literature and policy reports). For each case, data extracted focused on: (1) the financing mechanism employed, (2) how funds were raised and allocated, (3) documented outcomes or impacts on surgical access or health system financing and (4) any reported challenges and opportunities specific to surgical care. Extracted information was synthesised narratively, with cases compared within and across financing mechanisms to identify common themes, contextual enablers and barriers relevant to expanding the domestic fiscal space for surgical care. The illustrative cases sought to provide practical examples of policy approaches that may help expand domestic fiscal space for surgical care, where possible.

## Results

The results are presented to first describe the scale of health expenditure and fiscal capacity in LMICs, then the sources and flow of domestic health financing and finally the allocation of these resources to surgical and non-surgical disease burden categories over time.

### Healthcare expenditure globally and fiscal capacity in LMICs

In 2021, global CHE totalled US$9.84 trillion (median=US$2.3 billion, IQR=US$15.6 billion), with average global CHE per capita at US$1383.85 (see online supplemental Table B1 for a complete ranked list of countries by CHE in 2021). From 2000 to 2021, global CHE increased by an average of US$333.13 billion per year, with an average annual change of 0.09% in CHE as a percentage of GDP. In terms of government spending, GGHED made up 53.66% of CHE globally, amounting to US$5.26 trillion (see online supplemental table B4 for country-level changes in GGHED over time). When measured as a percentage of GDP, CHE in LMICs was lower than in UMICs and HICs, while CHE in UMICs aligned with the global average16 (online supplemental figure 1; see online supplemental table B2 for a complete ranked list of countries).

#### Taxes

Taxes are mandatory financial charges levied by governments broadly on individuals, businesses or goods to fund general public expenditure, including healthcare. In the context of health, taxes can be general (allocated across multiple sectors) or earmarked for specific purposes, such as strengthening health systems or financing surgical care. Earmarked taxes provide a predictable and consistent revenue stream, particularly for targeted health interventions like disease control or infrastructure development.17 Common examples include sin taxes on tobacco, alcohol and sugary drinks as well as taxes on income, corporate profits or value-added goods.

Earmarking taxes for health, such as sin taxes or environmental levies, ensures predictable funding for health-specific initiatives but can constrain fiscal flexibility, particularly when unexpected health crises arise.18 The WHO highlights that poorly implemented earmarking can create rigidities in government budgets, leading to suboptimal allocations across health sectors. For instance, funds may be overly concentrated on one intervention, such as vaccinations, at the expense of broader health needs, including surgical care.18 The GH2050 report underscores that the lack of essential commodities, such as surgical instruments and anaesthesia supplies, is a key barrier to delivering timely and effective surgical services.19 Targeted earmarking for these commodities can help ensure consistent access to essential surgical services. Furthermore, sin taxes, which are frequently earmarked for health, can disproportionately impact low-income populations due to their regressive nature. Over time, as campaigns reduce consumption of taxed goods, such as tobacco or sugary drinks, the revenue generated from these taxes may decline, threatening the sustainability of funding.20

The WHO recommends earmarked taxes as complementary financing mechanisms linked to broader health objectives, such as UHC, with flexible frameworks to ensure fund reallocation to emerging priorities when necessary.18 Specifically, for surgical care financing, WHO suggests incorporating earmarked funds into a comprehensive health financing strategy that balances targeted spending with broader systemic strengthening. Additionally, governments should adopt progressive taxation models to mitigate the regressive impact of sin taxes, ensuring that low-income populations are not disproportionately burdened.17

#### Subsidies

Subsidies are financial contributions provided by governments to reduce the cost of healthcare services, making them more affordable for consumers, especially those in low-income groups. In healthcare, subsidies often target essential services such as maternal care, vaccinations and surgeries, reducing OOP costs and enhancing access for vulnerable populations. Subsidies are typically financed through general taxation or external donor support and are allocated to health insurance programmes or service delivery platforms.21 While subsidies improve affordability and access, they face challenges related to long-term sustainability and equitable distribution.22 Additionally, the quality of subsidised services may vary in resource-constrained settings, limiting their effectiveness. The allocation of subsidies may not always be equitable, with marginalised populations sometimes remaining underserved due to implementation challenges.23

#### Levies

Levies are special charges imposed by governments on specific goods, services or industries, often serving as an additional revenue stream earmarked for particular public purposes. These can include charges on natural resource extraction (eg, oil, gas, mining) or luxury goods, with revenues directed towards healthcare. In resource-rich countries, levies on extractive industries are commonly used to fund health initiatives, including infrastructure development for surgical services.24 Revenue volatility from fluctuating commodity prices poses a significant challenge, as healthcare funding becomes less predictable. Misallocation of funds, often due to corruption or weak governance, further reduces the effectiveness of levy-based financing in addressing surgical care gaps.24

#### OOP payments

OOP payments occur when individuals directly pay for healthcare services, typically at the time of use. This mechanism places the financial burden on patients and is often the primary source of healthcare financing in LMICs. High reliance on OOP payments leads to catastrophic health expenditures and inequitable access to care, particularly for costly interventions like surgeries.25 Health systems lacking financial risk protection are unsustainable for achieving universal health coverage.12

#### Insurance mechanisms

Health insurance plays a critical role in reducing financial barriers to healthcare and providing financial risk protection for populations. Through prepayment and risk pooling, insurance mechanisms mitigate the burden of OOP payments and ensure equitable access to healthcare, including surgeries. Insurance contributing to domestic resources can be categorised into three major types: community-based health insurance (CBHI), PHI or national health insurance (NHI), and SHI. Each model has unique characteristics.

#### National health insurance

NHI is a tax-funded universal system ensuring healthcare coverage, including surgeries, for all citizens. These systems aim to reduce financial barriers, improve equity and enhance financial protection by pooling resources to fund comprehensive care for the entire population. Thailand’s Universal Coverage Scheme significantly reduced OOP payments and expanded access to surgical care, especially in rural areas, but rising healthcare costs and demographic shifts challenge its sustainability.26 Similarly, Ghana’s NHI ensures broad access to essential surgical services but faces inequities between urban and rural areas.27 NHI systems achieve equity and financial protection but require robust funding mechanisms and measures to ensure equal access.

#### Community-based health insurance

CBHI pools resources at the community level to provide healthcare coverage, including surgeries. These schemes rely on voluntary contributions from community members, which are aggregated into a shared fund, often supplemented by government subsidies or external donor support. While CBHI improves access to essential surgical services, high-cost procedures often remain uncovered due to financial constraints. Rwanda’s Mutuelles de Santé covers 90% of the population, improving access to surgeries like caesarean sections through subsidies.21 Senegal’s Couverture Maladie Universelle also includes CBHI but struggles to provide adequate surgical coverage for low-income groups due to financial and administrative constraints.28 While CBHI expands access in underserved areas, its limited coverage for high-cost surgeries and reliance on external funding pose challenges.

#### Social health insurance

SHI involves compulsory contributions from employees, employers and governments to fund healthcare, including surgeries. Contributions are typically deducted from salaries or funded through employer and government participation. Ghana’s National Health Insurance Scheme provides coverage for emergency surgeries like caesarean sections but faces delays in reimbursements that affect service delivery.27 Indonesia’s Jaminan Kesehatan Nasional offers universal coverage for surgeries but grapples with financial sustainability due to rising costs.29 SHI improves access to surgical care but requires efficient management to address increasing healthcare demands.

## Discussion

### Overview

Surgical care presents distinct financing challenges compared with other health services, as delivery of surgical and anaesthetic care requires substantial fixed and capital investments across infrastructure, equipment, supply chains and specialised workforce, which must be established before services can be delivered. These investments cannot be financed through incremental budget increases alone.1 In addition, essential surgical care is inherently cross-cutting, contributing to the management of NCDs, RMNCAH and trauma care, and therefore does not align easily with vertical, disease-specific financing models, necessitating coordinated, system-wide public investment.1 2

This landscape review describes the current patterns and mechanisms of domestic resource mobilisation for health, with a particular focus on LMICs. Three key findings emerge: (1) domestic resources form the majority of CHE, while LMICs rely disproportionately on OOP payments and external financing; (2) domestic spending on surgical services, as approximated using the SES, has not increased relative to CD spending in LMICs despite the growing disease burden and (3) several fiscal mechanisms for expanding domestic fiscal space exist as options for countries to employ.

### Strengthening domestic resource allocation for surgical care

Governments are responsible for ensuring equitable access to health services, particularly in contexts where market mechanisms fail to deliver affordable care.30 However, with declining availability of external resources and donor funding, the imperative to expand domestic fiscal space has become increasingly urgent.30

Our findings emphasise the central role of domestic resources in health system financing, with GHE contributing a global median of 53.7% of CHE. However, LMICs allocated a median of only 34.9%, highlighting inequities in resource mobilisation. These regions also exhibit higher reliance on external funding and OOP payments. Such reliance undermines financial protection and exacerbates inequalities in access to care, particularly for resource-intensive interventions like surgery.12 For patients, this often translates into delayed care, asset depletion or foregone treatment, reinforcing cycles of poverty when surgical care is needed. Despite modest increases in the proportion of national budgets allocated to health globally, LMICs remain below global benchmarks such as the 2001 Abuja Declaration target of 15%.31 Tracing fund flows using global aggregate values for 2021 revealed that the domestic sector produced the majority of revenue (75.8%) and mobilised the majority of fiscal resources (61.89%), with very little revenue from external sources (0.27%) (figure 2).

While strengthening domestic resource mobilisation is essential for sustainable financing, external financing remains a critical complement in many LMICs, particularly given fiscal constraints and competing development priorities. Multilateral institutions and HICs have an important role in supporting surgical system strengthening through long-term investments that reduce reliance on OOP payments.

### Surgical allocation trends

The SES provides an upper-bound proxy for surgical expenditure derived from GHED disease-burden categories. Globally, SES categories—comprising NCDs, RMNCAH and injuries—received similar proportions of CHE as CDs. The prioritisation of CDs in LMICs reflects persistent historical funding trends driven by external funding interests, earmarking and agenda setting. These gaps underscore the need for more granular surgical spending indicators within GHED.

### Fiscal mechanisms for increasing domestic resources for surgery

We identified several fiscal mechanisms used in LMICs to address funding gaps and expand domestic fiscal space for health. Strengthening domestic financing for surgical care must address the dual challenges of sustainability and equity. Fiscal policies, such as progressive taxation, PHI and targeted levies, should support comprehensive service delivery without exacerbating inequalities.18

Taxes, including sin taxes on tobacco, alcohol and sugary beverages, have proven effective in generating revenue for health-specific initiatives. For instance, Mexico’s sugar-sweetened beverage tax reduced consumption and generated additional health funds.20 When assessed purely in terms of tax incidence, these taxes often have regressive impacts, disproportionately affecting lower income populations, with limited earmarking for surgical care and significant industry resistance.32 However, extended cost-effectiveness and welfare analyses demonstrate that lower income populations often experience larger consumption reductions and health gains, while higher income groups may bear a greater share of the long-term economic burden.33 Subsidies, like Rwanda’s CBHI (Mutuelles de Santé), reduce financial barriers and enhance access to essential services, including surgical care.21 However, their reliance on donor support raises sustainability concerns.

PHI systems, whether social, national or community-based, offer structured resource allocation but face challenges like delayed reimbursements, inequitable access and rising costs, limiting their ability to improve surgical access.34 National insurance schemes like India’s Ayushman Bharat have expanded insurance coverage for low-income households, including surgical services, but face shared challenges including rising healthcare costs, reimbursement delays and inequitable access in rural areas.34

Despite these challenges, fiscal mechanisms offer opportunities for governments to expand their fiscal space and enhance financial protection. Improved earmarking of tax revenues, particularly for NCDs, RMNCAH, trauma and injuries—conditions that comprise the SES—could significantly strengthen GHE and CHE. As our findings suggest, domestic resources currently contribute the majority of CHE globally, yet this proportion remains substantially lower in LMICs.

The case studies indicate that public and SHI systems provide the strongest foundation for financing surgical care through prepayment and risk pooling, while health-specific taxes represent the most feasible sources of new domestic revenue. However, the SES analysis indicates that surgery remains underprioritised within existing government health budgets, underscoring the importance of improving allocation alongside mobilising new funds. These findings highlight the need to prioritise both mobilisation and allocation of domestic resources to ensure sustainable financing for surgical care, particularly in LMICs.35

### Policy implications and recommendations

To achieve UHC and address the surgical burden, policymakers should prioritise three complementary health strategies: expanding public and SHI coverage for surgical services, using health-specific taxes to generate domestic revenue for surgical interventions and establishing reportable measures of surgical expenditure within the WHO GHED. Equity considerations should be evaluated across financial, behavioural and health outcomes when designing and assessing fiscal policies for surgical care financing. Expanding financial protection for surgical care is critical: 3.7 billion people risk catastrophic health expenditure if surgery is required, and 33 million experience it annually.1 Reducing OOP costs for surgical care, through UHC-aligned insurance mechanisms, disproportionately benefits the poorest households by lowering the risk of impoverishment and financial hardship.36 Strengthening domestic financing for surgical care is not only a health system imperative, but a critical mechanism for protecting patients from poverty and advancing equitable UHC.

NSPs offer a government-led strategic framework that outlines country-specific priorities with a defined budget and targets across the surgical system. Early adopters have demonstrated that NSPs can elevate surgery within a national health agenda, improve collaboration between ministries of health and finance and ensure sustainable financing.37 Furthermore, global health organisations should support the development of standardised surgical outcome indicators to enhance accountability and evidence-based decision-making.1 This analysis aligns with WHA Resolutions 68.15 and 72.16 and supports the implementation of strategies such as the ECO Strategy and Action Plan (2026–2035) for sustainable and scalable ECO care.

### Limitations and future directions

This review is limited by the absence of direct surgical expenditure data and reliance on the SES as a proxy measure for surgical spending. The SES assumes that expenditure allocated to NCDs, RMNCAH and trauma and injuries reasonably approximates surgical expenditure; however, proportions of spending within these categories support non-surgical care. Recent estimates suggest that operative conditions, defined through expert consensus as those potentially requiring management by a surgically trained provider, account for approximately 28.1% of the combined DALY burden attributable to NCDs, RMNCAH and trauma and injuries.15 These estimates reflect disease burden rather than healthcare utilisation or financial expenditure. Accordingly, the SES overestimates surgical expenditure, suggesting that the true disparity in financial allocation may be larger.

Additionally, GHED reporting completeness varies across countries and years, with some countries reporting data for less granular variables; although more recent years with substantially incomplete datasets were excluded, residual heterogeneity in reporting depth may further constrain the generalisability of findings. Some potential financing mechanisms, such as government borrowing or service-related fees, are not systematically captured as distinct sources within the GHED framework and were, therefore, beyond the scope of this analysis. Health expenditure patterns during the COVID-19 pandemic may differ from prepandemic trends, and future analyses could examine pandemic-specific shifts as more complete post-2021 data become available. In addition, future research should prioritise development of granular surgical financing indicators, evaluation of the cost-effectiveness of fiscal mechanisms and exploration of innovative financing models for surgical care. Addressing these gaps is critical to advancing equitable and sustainable surgical systems globally.

## Conclusion

Strengthening domestic financing through targeted fiscal policies and improved resource allocation can enhance access to surgical care and health system independence in LMICs. NSPs and better reporting metrics are critical to integrating surgical care into UHC strategies.

Surgical conditions account for approximately one third of the global burden of disease. In 2025 at least 160 million additional operations per year were needed to meet this need, which is greatest in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Standardizing surgical packages is a key step toward improving operating room (OR) eﬃciency and expanding surgical care delivery across high-, middle-, and low-resource settings. Yet in low-resource settings, surgical equipment procurement often remains fragmented, non-standardized, and driven by facility-level ad-hoc processes rather than procedure-based planning. A universal standard could support high-quality surgical care that is both nationally scalable and internationally consistent. The World Health Organization’s (WHO) service package delivery and implementation (SPDI) tool is a viable candidate for such standardization of surgical instrument sets as it already covers nearly all essential surgeries identiﬁed by existing normative frameworks, making it a strong foundation for universal surgical package standardization. National implementation of reduced, standardized surgical sets could extend demonstrated single-center eﬃciency gains by improving OR eﬃciency and increasing case volume, supporting case reproducibility and more consistent care, and making supply chains more reliable, cost-eﬀective, and environmentally sustainable. Pre-deﬁned packages lend themselves to rapid, cost-eﬀective scale-up of supply chains, while minimized sets can also lower the carbon emissions associated with surgical care. Ministries of health, hospital networks, and practitioners at the facility level may consider the WHO’s UHC Compendium as a foundation for expanding access to safe, high-quality surgical care.

## 1 Introduction

Surgical conditions are thought to account for 28%−32% of the overall global burden of disease (1). In 2025, at least 160 million additional operations per year were needed to meet this burden (2). Health systems can avert associated mortality by providing patients with safe, timely, and aﬀordable surgical care. To deliver this standard of care, they must maintain the necessary infrastructural and operational capacity. Surgical service delivery relies on multiple interrelated factors, including expedient patient transport, appropriate diagnostics, operative room availability, surgical equipment and supplies, human resources, intensive care capabilities, and other essential services. In addition to workforce and infrastructure, health systems must also operationalize processes that, when optimized, ensure maximal service delivery and improve patient outcomes. Standardizing surgical packages is a key step to improving operating room (OR) eﬃciency and expanding surgical care delivery across high-, middle-, and low-resource settings. Surgical packages are itemized descriptions of the supplies required for a given operation, including the diagnostics, surgical medical equipment, consumables, and sterile surgical instruments. The creation of optimized surgical sets, also known as surgical trays, has been protocolized at many independent centers, yet universally standard sets that transcend geographic, rural-urban, and resource-diverse contexts have remained largely aspirational. A universal standard could support high-quality care that is nationally scalable and internationally consistent. In many lowresource settings, procurement is fragmented, non-standardized, and driven by facility-level ad-hoc processes rather than procedurebased planning. As a result, what is available in the operating room may reﬂect what was requested or procured sporadically, rather than what is required for safe and eﬃcient care. Globally transparent and rational procurement practices can be enhanced by standardized WHO tools. The Universal Health Coverage Compendium (UHC-C) houses an extensive catalog of medical and surgical packages. Its service package delivery and implementation (SPDI) tool allows user countries to select packages for inclusion in their national health service plans.1

The medical devices (i.e., diagnostics, medical equipment and surgical instruments) are taken from the WHO medical devices information system (MeDevIS) and the surgical sets listed in the WHO medical devices packages (MeDevPacks). One example amongst its 91 surgical instrument sets is the non-consumable laparotomy instrument set, which outlines the speciﬁc technical characteristics (e.g., shape, angle, edge, material) and quantities of forceps, needle holders, retractors, scissors, and other instruments. The MoSCoW prioritization framework was used to streamline the essential instruments that are required for a given procedure, whereas the “Must Do, Should Do, and Can Do” framework described below was used to identify which procedures are the highest priority for ﬁrst-level care.

## 2 Approach and outcomes

At a minimum, a global standardization tool must adequately cover essential surgeries. Low-resource health systems often require clinicians to prioritize a select group of essential surgical procedures in the ﬁrst-level hospital setting. Two frameworks that identify priority operations are: (1) The third edition of the Disease Control Priorities’ (DCP3) essential surgeries and, (2) The Lancet Commission on Global Surgery’s (LCoGS) “Must Do, Should Do, and Can Do” operations (3, 4). To test the coverage of the SPDI tool, each procedure from both frameworks was queried in the SPDI platform to assess whether an SPDI entry and surgical instrument set were present. Twenty-nine of 44 DCP3 procedures had entries with embedded instrument sets. Of the LCoGS-identiﬁed procedures, 4/5 “must do,” 6/8 “should do,” and 3/8 “can do” procedures had entries with embedded instrument sets (Table 1). For procedures lacking a SPDI entry with an associated instrument set, the authors conducted a qualitative review and assigned the procedures to one of three categories:

1. No SPDI entry exists, but coverage is achieved by an alternative existing instrument set [e.g., superﬁcial abscess drainage (incision and drainage surgery set), drainage of dental abscess (dental surgery tray)]; n = 10. 2. An SPDI entry exists with an embedded surgical set that is not yet accessible due to a pending website update [e.g., dilation and evacuation (vacuum aspiration set)], n = 2. 3. An SPDI entry exists but lacks an embedded surgical set; coverage is achieved by an alternative existing surgical set [e.g., tubal ligation (gynecology set), colostomy creation (abdominal surgery set)], n = 10.

Apart from a single procedure, uretero-renoscopy, all essential surgeries identiﬁed by Disease Control Priorities 3 and the Lancet Commission on Global Surgery were either explicitly built into the SPDI tool or indirectly included in existing alternative surgical sets per qualitative evaluation. This breadth of coverage positions the SPDI tool as a strong candidate for universal standardization.

## 3 Discussion

Universal standardized packages are expected to oﬀer the beneﬁts of improving operative eﬃciency, reproducibility, costeﬀectiveness, and environmental sustainability. Ultimately, these advantages are expected to support high-quality patient care and more reliable supply chains. Importantly, standardized packages should function as minimum system-level standards rather than ﬁxed or exhaustive requirements, with surgical care providers retaining discretion to request clinically justiﬁed additions.

### 3.1 Improve operative room eﬃciency to increase case volume

Standardized surgical packages are expected to make operating rooms more eﬃcient. Because the UHC-C surgical sets are optimized in both composition and quantity, instruments can be strategically allocated across sets without compromising safety. This more judicious distribution of instruments enables the following proven approaches to increase eﬃciency: streamlining tray assembly and sterilization, expediting operating room turnover, and reducing intra-operative time (5). Evaluation of optimized trays for four head and neck

procedures demonstrated a 58% to 66% (P < 0.05) decrease in assembly time and 26% to 37% (P < 0.05) decrease in OR setup time (6). Using a Lean 5S methodology (sort, simplify, sweep, standardize, self-discipline), setup time for minimallyinvasive spine surgery decreased by 37% (13.1–8.2 min, p = 0.0015) (7). Eﬃcient operative rooms with high surgical throughput are likely to reduce surgical waiting times and delays in essential surgical care. National implementation of reduced surgical sets could extend these single-center eﬃciency gains. Thus, these eﬃciency gains could support improved surgical access beyond individual patients to entire populations.

### 3.2 Facilitate case reproducibility to ensure quality

Operative consistency may promote outcome consistency, an indicator of high-quality care. When centers standardize surgical equipment, surgical preparation can become more reproducible. Adopting the UHC Compendium’s packages into operative practice is expected to make the medications, team compositions, consumable supplies, instruments, and OR equipment more consistent across cases. This may have additional use cases in conﬂict zone areas where inventories are often disrupted. Making operations reproducible may also simplify training particularly in remote settings where basic surgery is frequently task-shifted to generalist clinicians or in academic settings where residents are acquiring new operative skills. Furthermore, standardized surgical processes, such as the WHO surgical safety checklist, have been associated with lower postoperative complications and peri-operative mortality (8). In the same vein, standardized surgical packages may reduce workﬂow variability and opportunities for error, although their direct eﬀects on patient outcomes require further evaluation.

### 3.3 Make supply chains reliable, cost-eﬀective, and environmentally sustainable

Standardizing surgical equipment may facilitate rapid, cost-eﬀective, and environmentally sustainable scale up of surgical service delivery. Optimized surgical sets can help health ministries to mitigate widespread supply chain shortages. A necessary ﬁrst step is to deﬁne a minimum service standard for essential equipment. The UHC Compendium established minimum standards using expert clinician review. The program harnessed the technical discretion of 20 surgical faculty members across variable resource contexts to determine the optimal lean composition of each surgical package. Standard, lean packages can then streamline supply chain processes. Thus, equipment availability may not actually be a luxury, but the product of a systematized standardization strategy. Minimizing surgical sets can rationalize instrument use and reduce health system costs (9). Such cost savings may reduce ﬁnancial pressure on health systems. Whether they translate into lower costs for patients requires further evaluation. Reducing surgical equipment lowers the environmental burden from consumable use and sterilizing non-consumable instruments. Like many other single-center studies, a tray reduction program in the UK found that reducing surgical trays by about 50% for pediatric open herniotomy was associated with an annual reduction of approximately 384 kgCO2 emissions (10). If adopted at scale, standardized surgical sets could contribute to reductions in health care system carbon emissions.

### 3.4 Change as a downhill battle

Change is always met with resistance. Challenging surgical care providers to deviate from the trays they are accustomed to is no exception. However, it is worth clarifying what standardization does and does not mean in this context. Standardized packages are primarily a system-level intervention designed for health ministries, hospital administrators, and supply chain planners to deﬁne minimum standards, streamline procurement, and expand access. They are not meant to supersede the clinical judgement of individual surgical care providers, who must retain ﬂexibility to adapt standardized packages to particular patients, procedures, or clinical situations. However, at the system level, surgical care providers may very well covet having access to consistently complete trays, expedited OR turnover times, and a reduced carbon footprint more than they grieve personalized surgical trays.

## 4 Conclusion

Standardized surgical packages are expected to promote OR eﬃciency, case reproducibility, and high-quality patient care. Pre-deﬁned sets of medications, instruments, and operative equipment lend themselves to rapid, cost-eﬀective scale-up of supply chains. Minimized sets can also lower the carbon emissions associated with surgical care. Ministries of health, hospital networks, and practitioners at the facility level may consider the WHO’s UHC Compendium as a foundation for surgical care expansion, while allowing adaptation to local context and individual clinical judgement.

Introduction Surgical care is an essential component of any functioning health system (1–3). Conditions requiring surgical care account for nearly one-third of the global disease burden, meaning health equity is not achievable without access to safe, timely, affordable surgical care (3,4). These conditions include noncommunicable diseases such as cancers, trauma and injury, and maternal and child health (4). Effective surgical systems are essential for reducing preventable morbidity and mortality, and achieving broader health system goals of universal health coverage (UHC) (3,5). Programs and policy interventions for strengthening surgical systems, such as National Surgical Plans (NSPs), rely on robust monitoring and evaluation frameworks to track progress and achieve targets. Indicators serve as measurable benchmarks to assess health system performance and tracking progress towards policy targets (6,7). Data collected from indicator tracking can be used as evidence to advocate for scarce human and capital resources needed to strengthen health systems and achieve the health-related Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), which also converge in 2030 (8,9). Unfortunately, the adoption and reporting of global surgery indicators have been inconsistent across countries, despite their anticipated value (3,7,10). In 2015, the Lancet Commission on Global Surgery (LCoGS) published a formative analysis on the global status of access to surgical care with corresponding targets for achieving Global Surgery 2030 (3). The commission identified six core indicators essential for achieving equitable surgical care access. The indicators span the domains of health service delivery, workforce, information systems, and economic impact. The LCoGS indicators reflect health system readiness and capacity to deliver high-quality surgical care to all when needed. Through an extensive consensus development process, these indicators were selected for their alignment with the core elements of UHC (access to surgical care, the provision of essential surgical services, and financial risk protection). The indicators provide insight into the preparedness of the health system to provide surgical services (geographic access to care, surgical workforce density), service delivery (surgical case volume provided, perioperative mortality rate), and the impact of surgical care on patients (catastrophic health expenditure) (10). Additionally, the indicators align with the WHO Health System Building Blocks framework  (11). Many of these indicators have been incorporated into the World Bank’s World Development Indicators (WDI) and the WHO 100 Core Global Health Indicators (6,12). While the LCoGS demonstrated the importance of the core surgical indicators for showing the capacity of a health system to provide surgical services, evidence is needed to determine if improvements in surgical care capacity, delivery, and quality/impact on population health have been made. The absence of highquality, country-level indicator data makes it almost impossible to meaningfully track progress towards global surgery targets and evaluate whether the targets laid out 10 years ago were appropriate and achievable at the outset. We are also unable to validate the current targets as they may over- or underestimate surgical need, capacity and quality through the generalized but not necessarily generalizable approach. Thus, there are two major gaps in our current knowledge of the global surgery indicators: we need an updated quantification of the current status of each indicator, and we need to improve our understanding of the practices surrounding data collection and reporting by all WHO member states. This is crucial for understanding the current state of global surgery and targeting interventions to improve surgical care access and meet the 2030 targets (Figure 1). The impact of the 2021 indicator definition updates on data collection, data reporting, and surgical policy is unclear. For example, a systematic review of global surgery indicators within India, published in June 2023, showed that India did not meet the targets set by LCoGS for any of the indicators and that there was limited data for certain indicators- specifically geospatial access and economic impact (13). Additionally, there was variability in the evidence available for workforce density, surgical volumes, and POMR. This study showed a need for subnational district and state level data reporting as well as reporting between the public and private health sectors and different levels of care (13). For example, Brazil’s Unified Health System, (Sistema Único de Saúde, SUS), has implemented a robust data collection system that enables consistent reporting of surgical indicators (14). Other examples are linked closely to efforts to conduct a baseline assessment for the NSP development. Such was the case in the Pacific Region where 14 countries collected data on the first four of six indicators with data collection support from the Royal Australasian College of Surgeons and the Pacific Islands Surgical Association (15). In Ecuador and Namibia, similar nationwide baseline assessments that generated the indicators were conducted for the purpose of developing an NSP (16). Other countries appear to rely on retrospective record reviews to collect indicator data. For example, in Uganda, a standardized quantitative assessment and semi structured interview was administered to key stakeholders at 17 randomly selected public hospitals in order to gain insight on surgical indicator data (17). Interestingly, indicator reporting in HICs does not appear much better. The data relevant to the indicators may be accessible via ministries of health, other professional societies, or in reviews conducted by individuals groups but this data is not often synthesized and reported at a national level (12). The variability and sporadic nature of surgical indicator reporting within and across countries shows a need to improve our understanding about current practices (7). The recommendation in LCoGS was for annual reporting to enable consistent monitoring and evaluation of NSPs and health system strengthening in general. Challenges in reporting also stem from the heterogeneity in the indicator definitions and methodologies (Table 1). We expect many factors cited as facilitators and barriers to NSP development, such as financing, stakeholder engagement and political will, affect surgical indicator reporting as well (18). While much of the existing data mentioned is reported at a subnational level, or not routinely reported, understanding the methods that have facilitated success may help us scale up and expand efforts to understand the status of surgical indicators and access. Given the need for evidence-based policies, data-driven health systems strengthening, and the fastapproaching Global Surgery 2030 targets, the scoping review aims to provide a comprehensive status update on progress towards equitable surgical care access by quantifying the core indicators. The review will provide critical insights into reporting practices, including where reporting takes place, how and where reporting occurs, how the indicators are used, and facilitators and barriers to reporting. Additionally, the review aims to provide recommendations to inform future policy development, increase reporting rates and help develop strategies for data collection and surgical care access (7). Improved indicator reporting has the potential to accelerate our progress towards Global Surgery 2030 goals and to establish more effective and equitable targets for the future. Determining the research question The research team convened a group of experts with experience developing and evaluating the LCoGS indicators. Many in the group were involved in the initial systematic reviews, consensus development, and synthesis studies when the indicators were first proposed in 2015 and reviewed in 2021. During the meetings, the group raised questions about the current status of surgical indicators and discussed the various proposed and current methods for determining each indicator. The group reflected on the process surrounding the first ‘status report’ for each indicator at the time of LCoGS and reflected on the documented and experienced challenges in reporting and monitoring the indicators. The group focused on possible facilitators and barriers to collecting and reporting indicator data and reflected on experiences from different regions where members have directly been involved in indicator collection, review or analysis. Inclusion Criteria The inclusion criteria for this scoping review uses the JBI definitions for population, concept, and context (20). Population Our review focuses on all populations. Any literature that reports at least one of the 5 LCoGS indicators for populations of all ages, sex, ethnicity or other demographic variables will be considered for inclusion. As the focus of the review is primarily on quantifying the indicators, the review will consider publications that report a critical component of the indicator, such as the numerator. Since we anticipate a low number of nationally representative publications, we will include publications that report data at a national, subnational or regional, and single facility level for manual estimation of the indicator where possible. Concept The main concept for our review is the quantification of the LCoGS indicators of access to safe, timely, affordable surgical care. The LCoGS indicators were first defined in the LCoGS in 2015. We will use the most recent, modified definitions developed through an Utstein process in 2021 as these are the most widely-accepted by the policy and academic global surgery communities (Table 1). To ensure consistency studies will be included in their descriptions mentioning either the LCoGS, the Utstein indicators, or both. The secondary concept pertains to the practices surrounding indicator reporting. This is described as possible facilitators or barriers to reporting global surgery indicators. If a study’s focus is on practices surrounding indicator reporting, the study will only be considered for inclusion if the study presents data that quantifies an indicator. Context This review will consider global surgery indicator reporting across geographic and health system settings. Any publication reporting at least one LCoGS indicator, in at least one WHO Member state will be eligible for inclusion. In addition to producing a global status report, these indicators serve the foundation for reporting and monitoring progress towards WHA Resolution 68.15 and more recently WHA 72.15 (21,22). Date range All relevant publications published before the end of 2024 will be included in the review. Types of Sources This scoping review will consider a broad range of literature sources reporting any quantitative, qualitative, mixed-method, experimental (e.g clinical trials) or observational (e.g. cohort or crosssectional) methods. We will include any study design. Qualitative studies will also be considered provided they present data relevant to both the primary and secondary objectives of this review. Grey literature will include unpublished research, conference abstracts, policy documents, databases, organizational reports and proceedings. Literature will be limited to publications in English.
